mcqs.question: What distinguishes interval DP's state dp[i][j] from the 2D state used in LCS or Edit Distance?
options: Both i and j index into the same underlying sequence, describing a contiguous subrange, rather than indexing two separate sequences being compared
Interval DP never needs a 2D table, only a 1D one
dp[i][j] in interval DP always represents a boolean reachability question
Interval DP requires j to always be less than i
mcqs.explanation: In LCS or Edit Distance, i and j are prefix lengths of two different strings. In interval DP, i and j are both positions within one sequence, marking the boundaries of a single contiguous subrange — that structural difference is exactly why the fill order has to change from row-by-row to length-by-length.

mcqs.question: Why must interval DP tables be filled in order of increasing interval length, rather than row by row?
options: Filling row by row is fine; length-based filling is only a stylistic preference

Because dp[i][j] depends on smaller subranges nested inside [i, j], and a longer interval can start at a smaller index than a shorter one — so row-by-row order doesn't guarantee dependencies are ready
Because the table must be square
Because interval DP always has fewer than n distinct lengths
mcqs.explanation: A length-3 interval starting at index 0 and a length-2 interval starting at index 5 can coexist, and row-by-row (by starting index) order provides no guarantee the shorter, nested intervals a cell depends on are already computed. Only ordering by increasing length guarantees every dependency is resolved first.

mcqs.question: In Burst Balloons, why does the recurrence consider balloon k as the LAST balloon burst in range [i, j], rather than the first?
options: Because balloons must be burst in a fixed left-to-right order

Because reasoning about the last burst means the range's boundary neighbors (balloons[i-1] and balloons[j+1]) never change regardless of what order the rest of the range is cleared in, keeping subproblems independent
Because bursting last always earns more coins than bursting first
There's no real difference — first-burst framing gives an identical recurrence
mcqs.explanation: Reasoning about which balloon bursts first means its neighbors depend on an arbitrary, shifting set of already-burst balloons elsewhere. Reasoning about which balloon bursts last guarantees everything else in the range is already gone, so its coin value always multiplies by the range's fixed outside boundaries.

mcqs.question: You're deriving an interval DP recurrence and notice each subproblem's effective boundaries keep shifting depending on an arbitrary order of earlier operations elsewhere in the range. What's the general fix?
options: Reframe the split around the LAST action taken within the interval instead of the first, so the remaining subproblems' boundaries become fixed
Switch from a 2D table to a 1D table
Increase the interval length considered at each step
Add memoization on top of the existing recurrence without changing its structure
mcqs.explanation: Naming this as 'reframe around the last action' is the general fix — as Burst Balloons shows, thinking about the last operation within a range makes everything else already-resolved, fixing the boundaries. Adding memoization to a recurrence with the wrong shape doesn't fix the underlying dependency problem.

mcqs.question: A Burst Balloons implementation crashes with an index-out-of-range error when computing dp[i][j] for the balloon at either end of the array. What's the likely fix?
options: Reduce the interval length considered by one
Switch the combine operation from max to min
Change the fill order from length-based back to row-based
Pad the balloons array with virtual boundary values (typically 1) on both ends, since balloons[i-1] and balloons[j+1] must be valid even when i is the first index or j is the last
mcqs.explanation: Burst Balloons' recurrence always references one index before i and one index after j, which don't exist at the array's true boundaries. Padding both ends with a virtual balloon of value 1 gives those references a valid, neutral value instead of running off the array.
